To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the protective effect of isoniazidisoniazid preventive therapypreventive therapy against tuberculosis was rapidly lost in a very high HIV-prevalence, high annual TB incidence setting.
the durability of protection against TB by 9-month IPT was lost in 6–12 months, and the observed rate was higher in the first year than the rate estimated from a mathematical model of trial outcomes.
the protection by IPT was short lived and the observed TB incidence rate after 12 months of IPT was higher than the estimated TB incidence rate after the end of IPT due to reinfections only.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the timing of the TB incidence after IPT in a high TB and HIV prevalence setting and associated risk factors.
the timing of tuberculosis after the completion of isoniazizd preventive therapy (Ipt) in a cohort of South African gold miners.
the timing of the TB disease after IPT and associated with the risk factors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
IPT is not a durable preventive strategy for the prevention of TB in this setting, and that the timing of the loss of protection is within 6–18 months after IPT.
IPT does not prevent TB for more than one year in a setting with very high TB prevalence and HIV prevalence, and that the protection is not due to sterilizing effect.
IPT provides protection against TB in the short term, but that the duration of protection is limited and that the mechanism is likely to be both reactivation and reinfection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
IPT is not sufficient in a setting with a high annual risk and HIV co-infection, and that a longer duration of IPT is warranted.
the protective effect of IPT was lost within the first 6–12 months, and that this was mainly due to reinfection.
the protection by IPT is lost within 6-12 months in high HIV prevalence settings with a high risk of infection.
The main takeaway from our work is that
TB incidence rates after IPT in high HIV prevalence settings are much higher than previously assumed and that this should be taken into account when designing and interpreting IPT studies.

the timing of TB disease after IPT in this setting was similar to that in other settings with a high annual risk for M. tuberculosis infection, and that the durability of protection was lost within 1 year.
the protection provided by IPT is not durable in a very high HIV and TB incidence setting and that the risk of TB disease increases rapidly after IPT stops.
